sec.p: Phase 1 (inflammation regulation, approximately 0–7 days post-surgery). This phase is characterized by an acute wound inflammatory response, with extensive infiltration of neutrophils and pro-inflammatory macrophages at the injury site and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species (ROS). The primary objective is to suppress excessive inflammation and establish a local microenvironment conducive to subsequent regeneration. In this model, the scaffold surface layer consists of a rapidly degradable chitosan/sodium β-glycerophosphate/gelatin thermosensitive hydrogel incorporating a matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-responsive crosslinker; anti-inflammatory miRNAs encapsulated in cationic polymer nanoparticles are dispersed within the hydrogel. MMPs highly expressed in the inflammatory microenvironment trigger crosslink cleavage, enabling rapid release within days to match the inflammation-regulation phase. Candidate anti-inflammatory miRNAs for this phase include miR-146a, which suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion by targeting IRAK1 in an inflammatory environment, and miR-27a-5p, which suppresses bacterially induced inflammatory responses by targeting PTEN.

Phase 2 (osteogenic–vascular coupling and regeneration, approximately 7–28 days post-surgery). As inflammation gradually resolves, the wound enters the proliferative repair phase, and local macrophages shift from a predominantly pro-inflammatory state toward reparative and regenerative states (see Section 3.2.1). Beyond secreting anti-inflammatory and reparative factors such as IL-10, they help establish a growth factor-enriched repair microenvironment through intercellular communication with other cells. Osteoblast differentiation, extracellular matrix deposition, and neovascularization proceed simultaneously, making this a critical window for periodontal tissue reconstruction. The middle scaffold layer incorporates poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanocarriers loaded with osteogenic and pro-angiogenic miRNAs; adjustment of polymer molecular weight and the lactide/glycolide (LA/GA) ratio enables sustained release over several weeks to match this phase. Candidate miRNAs include miR-21, which promotes osteogenic differentiation through the PI3K/AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin pathway, and miR-210, which upregulates VEGF expression.

Phase 3 (tissue maturation and remodeling, approximately 1–6 months post-surgery). This phase is characterized by tissue maturation and remodeling, during which regenerated tissue undergoes ordered alignment and mineralization under functional loading (e.g., occlusal forces), leading to periodontal ligament fiber reattachment and trabecular bone remodeling. The inner scaffold layer consists of a three-dimensionally printed β-TCP/hydroxyapatite (HA) ceramic core coated with a polymeric sustained-release film loaded with functional miRNAs; slow degradation of the ceramic matrix provides release over weeks to months. The mechanical support of the ceramic core simultaneously transmits physiological occlusal forces, promoting oriented alignment and mineralization of regenerated tissue through mechanotransduction. Mechanosensitive miRNAs in this phase include miR-21, which responds to mechanical tensile stimulation and regulates osteogenic differentiation of human PDLSCs by targeting ACVR2B (activin type IIB receptor), and miR-26a, for which the RUNX1/miR-26a/JAG1 axis inhibits osteoclastogenesis under compressive conditions.

The three-phase candidate miRNA combinations above are theoretical examples that may be replaced or expanded in the future according to specific research contexts and high-throughput screening results. The cross-stage use of miR-21, in particular, illustrates the principle of functional transition of a single molecule across repair phases: its net effect may depend on the microenvironmental context. In Phase 2, growth-factor accumulation in the defect activates the PI3K/AKT pathway, and miR-21 then exerts primarily osteogenic rather than anti-osteogenic effects (see Section 3.1). In Phase 3, superimposed mechanical stimulation directs it to target ACVR2B, further enhancing osteogenesis (37). Although this microenvironment-driven “dominant target selection” mechanism requires further experimental validation, it embodies the core value of the model’s temporally controlled release design—namely, aligning with the natural rhythm of tissue repair so that exogenous miRNAs exert their intended dominant regenerative effects at specific phases.

To evaluate the performance of this delivery system, we propose a multi-level evaluation framework encompassing in vitro release kinetics, in vitro biological functional validation, and in vivo tracking and efficacy assessment. At the in vitro level, the dialysis bag method or a constant-temperature shaking method would first be used, with key monitoring points at days 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 56, and 90, to quantify the release behavior of fluorescently labeled miRNAs and characterize the temporal release kinetics corresponding to the three-phase window. Pathway-specific reporter cell lines and functional assays would then be used to verify the biological activity of the released agents in a phase-specific manner. In Phase 1 (inflammation regulation), the pathway-inhibitory efficacy of anti-inflammatory miRNAs would be verified using an LPS-stimulated NF-κB luciferase reporter system. In Phase 2 (osteogenic–vascular coupling and regeneration), osteogenic activity would be assessed with a RUNX2 reporter system combined with ALP activity and alizarin red staining, supplemented by endothelial tubule-formation assays to evaluate pro-angiogenic effects. In Phase 3 (tissue maturation and remodeling), the osteogenic and anti-osteoclastic effects of miRNAs under mechanical loading would be evaluated using a Flexcell loading system together with tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining and osteogenic marker assays. At the in vivo level, fluorescently labeled miRNA mimics combined with in vivo imaging would first be used to monitor overall release trends; tissue sections collected at successive time points would be examined by fluorescence microscopy for residual drug and distribution across scaffold layers to elucidate in vivo temporal release patterns. Histological efficacy would then be evaluated in three phases: in Phase 1, local inflammatory cytokine levels and macrophage functional-state distribution would be assessed; in Phase 2, neovascularization and early osteogenesis would be evaluated by histology and immunohistochemistry; and in Phase 3, micro-CT would be used to quantify bone volume fraction (BV/TV), bone mineral density (BMD), and trabecular microstructural parameters, combined with histological assessment of periodontal ligament fiber reattachment and functional cementum–alveolar bone healing, thereby validating the potential of this sequential-release strategy for temporally coordinated synergistic therapy from an integrated perspective.

In summary, this review seeks to overcome the fragmentation of existing research on miRNA-mediated regulation of periodontal immune homeostasis and tissue regeneration and has preliminarily established an integrated analytical framework spanning molecular regulatory networks, smart delivery systems, and temporally coordinated regeneration models. The proposed spatiotemporally coordinated model offers a new theoretical basis for shifting the field from single-target intervention toward multi-network temporal regulation. With the continued refinement of multi-omics technologies, smart biomaterials, and large-animal validation systems, miRNA-based immunomodulatory therapies are expected to accelerate the translation from basic research to clinical application, opening new therapeutic avenues for functional periodontal tissue regeneration.
